Topic: What did Prospero's decision to drown his book cost the imagination he spent the whole play cultivating?
Montaigne — Judgement:
Prospero spent twelve years turning his island into a book he could rewrite at will — tempests, marriages, revenge — and I recognize the temptation, having retired to my own tower to govern a small kingdom of paper.

But my essays taught me that the self which studies itself keeps changing in the studying — "I cannot fix my object; it goes always tottering with a natural drunkenness" — and that any mastery requiring spirits and staffs is not knowledge but flight from one's own unsteadiness. Prospero's art let him command tempests he could never have commanded in his own household as a young duke; drowning the book does not cost him imagination, it costs him only the alibi imagination gave him for avoiding himself.

He loses nothing but the excuse, and gains only what was always the harder art — meeting Milan, and his own mortality, unassisted.

*The staff that commands the sea cannot teach a man to command his own unsteady heart.*
Austen — Judgement:
Society is a machine for turning improvisation into obedience, and Prospero's island was the last workshop where he still controlled the terms.

I have said that imagination untethered from social judgement is merely fancy, indulgence without consequence—Prospero's art on the island was exactly this: absolute power exercised where no one could refuse him, where Ariel must obey and Caliban must serve. Breaking the staff and drowning the book is not a renunciation of imagination but a surrender of it to circumstance, the same surrender every one of my heroines must make when the ball ends and the settlement begins. He trades a magic that answered only to his will for a Milan that will answer to nobody's—least of all his own contrivance.

He has not matured; he has simply run out of island.

*The imagination we praise as wisdom is often only the power we can no longer afford to keep.*
Camus — Judgement:
Prospero's final act is the oldest surrender dressed as wisdom: the belief that peace requires amputating the very faculty that made a man dangerous, made him fully alive.

His imagination was never mere stagecraft — the tempests, the spirits, the whole conjured isle were his revolt against an unjust exile, his refusal to accept the world as given. To drown the book is to mistake pardon for absolution, to trade the created world for the merely inherited one, as though forgiving his enemies discharges a debt reality never agreed to owe him. This is not maturity. It is exhaustion wearing maturity's mask — the same fatigue that tempts every rebel to lay down arms one battle short of transformation, settling for reconciliation because revolt has grown heavy.

Prospero does not renounce magic; he renounces the self that dared create against the given order, and dies a duke instead of living as a magus.

*The man who drowns his power to forgive his enemies has only discovered a quieter way to punish himself.*
Bashō — Judgement:
Prospero's book was never the wellspring — it was a walking stick he leaned on so long he forgot his legs still worked. Its drowning costs him nothing that was ever really his to keep.

I burned my hut before the road to the deep north and found I walked lighter for it. The imagination that filled that island — the tempest raised, the spirits sent running, the marriage staged, the enemies forgiven — never lived inside the pages. It lived in the doing, moment by moment, and moments cannot be bound in leather or drowned in fathoms. What Prospero surrenders is only his fear of standing empty-handed before what he made; the making itself has already passed, as all things pass, into the sea he's staring at.

The cost is nothing — the drowning is the last and finest proof the imagination was real.

*The staff that carried me up the mountain, I leave at its foot — the mountain, not the staff, was always mine.*
